title: Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018) — the CSLI warrant rule
citations: United States v. Carpenter, 913 F.3d 592 (6th Cir. 2019)
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. The Supreme Court held 5-4 that accessing seven or more days of historical cell-site location information (CSLI) is a Fourth Amendment search requiring a warrant supported by probable cause. Timothy Carpenter's robbery prosecution rested on 127 days of CSLI obtained under a 2703(d) court order; the Court ruled the third-party doctrine of Smith v. Maryland and United States v. Miller does not extend to the "exhaustive chronicle of location information" that CSLI reveals. Chief Justice Roberts wrote that CSLI is "detailed, encyclopedic, and effortlessly compiled," implicating deep privacy concerns. The decision left open real-time CSLI, tower dumps, and shorter periods. On remand the Sixth Circuit applied the good-faith exception and affirmed the conviction, 913 F.3d 592 (6th Cir. 2019). title: United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012) — GPS tracking as a search
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. The Supreme Court unanimously held that attaching a GPS device to a vehicle and tracking its movements for 28 days is a Fourth Amendment search. Jones is the bridge case between beeper-era law (Knotts, Karo) and the CSLI era. title: Smith v. Maryland, 442 U.S. 735 (1979) — the third-party doctrine origin
body: Public edition. Public legal record, fact-checked reference. Carpenter narrowed — but did not overrule — this doctrine for CSLI, distinguishing the "exhaustive chronicle" of location data from the limited business records at issue in Smith.
